new_statements.rule_in_words: Barupu is a word-tone language (five lexical tone classes L, H, LH, HL, HLH) with predictable, non-contrastive stress on the penultimate syllable of the word: a left-headed binary foot is built at the right edge of the word (only the final two syllables are footed, so trisyllables and longer words stress the penult). The lexical tone melody docks on the stressed penult and its last tone spreads one syllable rightwards, giving a pitch accent-like system. Stress is not weight-sensitive in monomorphemic words (final glide- or nasal-closed syllables do not attract it), but when suffix desyllabification or high-vowel deletion creates a closed final syllable, that syllable satisfies the foot and stress does not shift to the new penult (e.g. /k-a-te-i/ -> [kà.'tej], /k-a-te-ni/ -> [kà.'ten]). Stress is diagnosed phonetically by the slightly higher F0 and longer duration of the penult in L-class words (pp. 48-50), and by the mobility of rule-assigned tones under suffixation (pp. 50-57). The inflected word (prefixes + root + suffixes) is the stress domain; stress can fall on a prefix when the root desyllabifies (/k-a-te-a/ -> ['kà.tʃà], p. 51).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing); syllables other than the final two are described as 'always very short' (p. 49).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) A subset of words have an H or HL lexically linked to the penultimate or the final syllable ('lexically assigned' tones, surface melodies [H.L], [L.H], [L.HL]); these tones do not move with stress under suffixation (pp. 53-57). The lexically assigned final HL is explicitly noted as the exception to contour tones sitting on the stressed syllable (p. 50). (2) Morphophonological closed final syllables satisfy the foot so stress does not reassign (p. 51). (3) Some participant-adding suffixes carry their own tone and show sandhi with hosts (p. 39; §2.4.7). No mention of loanword exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the domain is the inflected phonological word including subject/mood prefixes and object suffixes (verbs) or the noun; examples are citation forms and elicited verb paradigms with F0 traces of single words. The thesis also notes tone interactions in compounds and phrases (§2.4.9) but gives no phrase-level stress rule. Stress is analysed as predictable and non-contrastive; the language is primarily tonal.
new_statements.identity_note: Corris 2005 describes the language of Barupu (formerly Warapu) village, which speakers officially call 'Bauni' (thesis p. 1); this is exactly Glottolog wara1302 'Bauni' (ISO bpe). Miller 2017 (LLM 35) later split the old ISO [wra] 'Warapu' into Bauni (Barupu/Pou villages), Uni (Ramo) and Bouni (Sumo); Corris's data are Bauni proper, from the main Barupu village site after the 1998 tsunami relocation. The thesis header on the repository says 2008 but the document itself is dated 2005 (Wikipedia editor note; the front matter downloaded here carries no other date).

tone_statements.quote: Barupu is a word tone language; words belong to tone classes in the lexicon. The five tone classes in Barupu are: L; H; LH; HL and HLH. There is, however, no distinction … between H and LH in monosyllabic words. … Polysyllabic words, however, display eight surface melodies. In the following sections I will argue that Barupu has penultimate stress and exemplifies a type of pitch accent system in which, for the majority of words, lexically specified tones are predictably attracted to the stressed syllable and then part or whole of the tone spreads one syllable to the right.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.4 'Suprasegmental phonology - tone and stress', pp. 38-39
tone_statements.summary: Word-tone language: five lexical melodies (L, H, LH, HL, HLH) dock on the stressed penult and spread right; some words fix H or HL on a syllable; predictable penultimate stress; HL downsteps after L.

tone_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2003. Morphological templates, headedness, and applicatives in Barupu. Oceanic Linguistics 42(1): 111-143.
tone_statements.quote: Word tone is not marked for the L, H, LH, and HL melodies (other than in 4.2.1), apart from the complex tones (LHL and HLH) when they are realized on just one syllable. … the monosyllabic ru’u ‘bird’ in example (6), which is a single syllable with a rise-fall pitch contour (see Crowther 2000 for a description of tonal contrasts in Barupu). … When two lexical nominals are compounded together, the tone of the unit is that of the right-most morpheme, spread over the whole word.
tone_statements.locator: p. 115 fn. 4 + p. 128 sec. 5.2.1 'Tone in compounds'
tone_statements.summary: Word-level tone melodies built from H and L: L, H, LH, HL, LHL, HLH (six); complex melodies surface as contours on monosyllables; in compounds the rightmost morpheme's melody spreads over the word.

tone_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1997. Tone systems in New Guinea. Linguistic Typology 1(3): 347-386.
tone_statements.quote: Syllable-level languages in the following section, from widely different parts of inea, all represent languages with a tone system that allows each ble in the word to bear a distinct tone. … In Sko (Voorhoeve 1971) there are three: ton high, low and rising, again independent of each other, with high and.J¢ tones appearing as falling tones phrase-finally. A similar system is for in Vanimo (Ross 1980; Donohue & Van Vugt 1992).
tone_statements.locator: p. 353 (sec. 3.1 'Syllable-level' opening) and p. 354 (end of sec. 3.1.1)
tone_statements.summary: Nothing on Barupu itself; for its Sko-family relatives Sko and Vanimo: three tones (high, low, rising), each syllable independently toned; high and low realised as falling phrase-finally.

sources.note: Language-survey paper (intelligibility, cognate percentages) splitting 'Warapu' into Bauni, Uni, Bouni. No stress statement; only remark on prosody is p. 14: 'Phonetically, Uni has at least two tones, high and low, and the tones contrast phonemically. Bauni has more.' The appendix wordlists (pp. 15-24) carry IPA stress marks (ˈ) on Bauni forms, mostly on the penult but not uniformly (e.g. ˈto.pa vs to.ˈpá 'stone', ni.ˈtú 'green coconut') and the author does not discuss them. The original langlxmelanesia.com URL is dead (HTTP 400); downloaded from the Internet Archive copy of 2020-07-12.

sources.note: Family overview only: Skou languages are tonal, with three to six tonal contrasts on a monosyllable and the morpheme as the domain of tone; Barupu's own inventory is not given here.

tone.quote: The languages of the Skou family are spoken along the north coast of New Guinea, from the Skou villages east of Humboldt Bay in Indonesia to Barupu west of Aitape in Papua New Guinea. … Tone and in most cases either unusual consonants or a high number of vowels feature prominently. Tonal contrasts range from three to six on a monosyllabic word, but in all well-investigated cases the domain of tone is the morpheme, not the syllable.
